html:
The Republic of Genoa was a sea power and banking state on the Ligurian coast of north-west Italy, from the early Middle Ages to 1797. The map shows it from 1600 to 1715, as a narrow strip of coast around its port.

Genoa grew rich from the crusades and the trade of the eastern Mediterranean. It held colonies at Galata by Constantinople, Kaffa in Crimea and the island of Chios, and fought long wars with Venice. It also beat Pisa at sea in 1284 and took Corsica. Christopher Columbus was a Genoese.

In 1528 the admiral Andrea Doria allied Genoa with Spain and gave it a new constitution. Its money power then peaked. The Bank of Saint George managed the state's debts, and Genoese bankers lent to the Spanish crown against American silver, settling accounts at the fairs of Piacenza. For about seventy years Genoa was the centre of European finance.

The republic sold Corsica to France in 1768. Napoleon turned it into the Ligurian Republic in 1797, and in 1815 it was given to the Kingdom of Sardinia.
